label: Institution
name: Bolshoi Kamenny Theatre
summary:
The Bolshoi Kamenny Theatre (Grand Stone Theatre) in St. Petersburg, Russia, was one of Imperial Russia's most prestigious opera houses, built in 1783-1784 and serving as the primary venue for opera and ballet performance in the Russian capital until its closure in 1886 and subsequent conversion to a conservatoire building. The theatre played a central role in the development of Russian classical music, hosting premieres of major Russian operas and ballets during the golden era of Imperial Russian culture.

The Bolshoi Kamenny (meaning 'Big Stone Theatre' to distinguish it from the Maly or 'Small' theatre) was built under Catherine the Great's cultural expansion program that sought to establish St. Petersburg as Europe's cultural rival. It hosted performances by visiting Italian opera companies that shaped Russian operatic taste, and later Russian premieres including works by Glinka, Dargomyzhsky, and other founders of Russian nationalist opera. The theatre's stone construction was notable in an era when most Russian theatres were wooden.

After the theatre's 1886 closure, its building was converted to house the St. Petersburg Conservatoire — the institution founded by Anton Rubinstein in 1862 that trained Tchaikovsky and remains Russia's premier music education institution. The building's conversion thus completed a symbolic handover from imported Italian opera to Russian classical music education — encapsulating the transition from European cultural dependency to Russian musical nationalism.
